column1: So India's whole mission... ten thousand crore, over five years.
Meta alone... thirteen lakh crore, in one single year.
That's not double.
That's more than a hundred times as much.
So is it hopeless?
No.
Because remember DeepSeek.
DeepSeek says it trained its base model on about two thousand chips.
Not hundreds of thousands.
And they were a cut-down version, made so they could still be sold to China.
So what's the lesson for you and me?
You don't always need the biggest room.
You need clever engineering.
And that's a game Indian engineers can play.
April twenty twenty-five.
The government picks the first company to build India's own model from scratch.
A Bengaluru startup called Sarvam.
Sarvam was started by two Indians you should know, Vivek Raghavan and Pratyush Kumar.
The mission gives them about four thousand of those Nvidia chips to work with.
But a month later, the doubts begin.
Sarvam's next model is built on top of a French one.
And critics ask — if the base is foreign, how is it Indian?
Fair question, isn't it?
You'd ask it too.
Can an Indian team train one from zero, start to finish, at home?
February twenty twenty-six.
Bharat Mandapam, Delhi.
The India A.I.
Impact Summit.
There, Sarvam shows India two new models.
The bigger one has a hundred and five billion parameters.
Think of them as tiny dials the machine tunes while it reads.
